issues.legal_issue: A mortgagor cannot seek a later accounting of the mortgagee’s net receipts from before the preliminary decree when those receipts should have been accounted for in determining the amount due under that decree.
material_facts: A mortgagee in possession brought a suit for sale to enforce the mortgage.
The preliminary decree declared the amount due without deducting the mortgagee’s net receipts from the property as required by the mortgagee’s accounting duty.
The mortgagors did not obtain an accounting of those pre-decree receipts before the preliminary decree was made and later sought one.
issues.conclusion: The claim for an accounting of receipts from before the preliminary decree was barred; the High Court’s direction to account for that period was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXXIV, rules 2 and 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must determine the amount due at the preliminary-decree stage when it declares that amount in the decree. Section 76(h) of the Transfer of Property Act requires the mortgagee’s net receipts to be credited against the mortgage debt. A preliminary decree is final as to matters that were directly and substantially in issue, or ought to have been raised, before it was made; a later claim is barred by res judicata. The Court also relied on section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Venkata Reddy v. Pethi Reddy.

predicates.mortgage_sale_suit: A mortgagee brought a suit seeking sale of mortgaged property to enforce the mortgage.
predicates.mortgagee_possessed_property: The mortgagee was in possession of the mortgaged property and received its profits.
predicates.pre_decree_receipts_not_credited: The amount declared due in the preliminary decree did not deduct the mortgagee’s net receipts from the property.
predicates.accounting_claim_not_raised_before_preli: The mortgagor did not obtain an accounting of those receipts before the preliminary decree was made.

issues.definition: When a mortgagee in possession receives property profits before a preliminary decree in a mortgage sale suit, and those receipts are not credited because an accounting claim was not raised before the decree, a later claim to account for them is barred.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgagee in possession must account for net receipts from the mortgaged property realized after the preliminary decree when the mortgage suit continues toward a final decree.
material_facts: The mortgagee remained in possession after the preliminary decree and received profits from the mortgaged properties.
The suit continued after the preliminary decree and required a final determination of the mortgagors’ liability.
The preliminary decree did not direct an accounting of receipts realized after it was made.
issues.conclusion: The post-decree net receipts had to be credited in fixing the mortgagors’ ultimate liability.
issues.legal_principle: Section 76(h) of the Transfer of Property Act imposes an accounting duty on a mortgagee in possession. A mortgage suit continues until the final decree, and the mortgagee’s statutory duty continues during that period. Payments made after the preliminary decree are taken into account in fixing the final mortgage liability; on the same analogy, the mortgagee’s net receipts after that decree must also be credited. The Court relied on Madan Theatres, Ltd. v. Dinshaw & Co. Ltd. and, with the stated limitation, Satyanarayana v. Suryanarayana.

predicates.mortgage_sale_suit: A mortgagee brought a suit seeking sale of mortgaged property to enforce the mortgage.
predicates.mortgagee_possession_continued_after_pre: The mortgagee remained in possession of the mortgaged property after the preliminary decree.
predicates.net_receipts_realized_after_preliminary_: The mortgagee received net profits from the mortgaged property after the preliminary decree.
predicates.suit_remained_pending_for_final_decree: The mortgage suit continued after the preliminary decree and had not yet reached its final decree.

issues.definition: If a mortgagee remains in possession and receives net profits after a preliminary decree while the mortgage suit continues, those profits must be credited in determining the final liability.

issues.legal_issue: A representation that a mortgagee will account for receipts does not estop the mortgagee from disputing a later accounting claim unless the mortgagor acted on the representation to their detriment.
material_facts: The mortgagee represented that he would account for receipts from the mortgaged properties.
The mortgagors deposited an amount toward the decretal liability and the mortgagee was permitted to withdraw it.
The amount deposited was less than the amount payable under the decree, and payment discharged a legal obligation and stopped interest from running on the amount paid.
issues.conclusion: The mortgagee was not estopped from disputing the accounting claim because the mortgagors suffered no detriment by acting on the representation.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 115 of the Evidence Act, estoppel requires a representation, action on the faith of that representation, and resulting detriment to the person who acted. The Court relied on C.D. Sugar Co. v. C.N. Steamship for the requirement of resulting detriment. Discharging an existing legal liability is not detrimental where the payment also secures a benefit, including stopping interest from running.

predicates.mortgage_sale_suit: A mortgagee brought a suit seeking sale of mortgaged property to enforce the mortgage.
predicates.mortgagee_represented_that_accounting_wo: The mortgagee told the mortgagor that an accounting of property receipts would be provided.
predicates.mortgagor_paid_in_reliance: The mortgagor made a payment after acting on the mortgagee’s representation.
predicates.payment_discharged_existing_legal_liabil: The payment went toward an amount the mortgagor was already legally required to pay.

issues.definition: When a mortgagor relies on the mortgagee’s promise to account by paying an amount already legally owed, that payment alone does not estop the mortgagee from disputing the accounting claim.
